notes.b: Access to education has widened across generations, so more children and adults now complete school and continue into further study.
points: Free second-level education was introduced from 1967, removing the fees that had kept many children from completing school.
Third-level tuition fees were abolished for eligible undergraduates from 1996, widening access to universities and institutes of technology.
A free pre-school year, the Early Childhood Care and Education scheme, gives every child access to early education before primary school.
Special needs assistants support pupils with special educational needs within mainstream classrooms.
The School Completion Programme targets students at risk of leaving school early, through homework clubs, breakfast clubs and individual school retention plans.
Leaving Certificate Applied is a modular, practical programme assessed over two years, preparing students for work and adult life.
Youthreach and Transition Year offer practical, work-based and personal development learning to young people in different circumstances.
Post Leaving Certificate courses and adult education give adults a second route to qualifications for work or further study.
The Higher Education Access Route, HEAR, improves third-level access for socially disadvantaged students, and DARE does the same for students with disabilities.
The Back to Education Allowance supports people on eligible social welfare payments to take approved courses.

notes.h: Effects of improved education on family life
points: Better-educated parents are better able to help with homework and to encourage children's achievement.
Women's education has increased their financial independence and their participation in paid employment.
Educational attainment affects job prospects and earnings, which in turn affect the standard of living of the family.
Adult education lets parents return to work after raising children, adding a second income to the household.

notes.h: Social welfare: purpose and types of payment
notes.b: Social welfare is income support paid by the state to people who are unemployed, sick, disabled, retired, widowed or caring for others.
points: Social insurance payments are funded by PRSI contributions from employees and employers, and depend on a record of contributions.
Means-tested payments depend on an assessment of household income and savings, so they are targeted at households in need.
Universal payments such as child benefit are paid for each child regardless of parental income.
Payments for lone parents and for low-income working families support parents who have the main responsibility for children.
A once-yearly clothing and footwear allowance helps families on low incomes meet the cost of school clothing.
Medical cards give eligible families access to free GP visits and prescribed medicines.
Welfare payments reduce child poverty by giving families a regular income when a parent is out of work or on a low wage.
Old age pensions give older people financial independence, reducing their dependence on adult children.
Carer's payments allow a family member to care for an elderly or disabled relative at home.
Conditions attached to many payments, such as job-seeking requirements, aim to prevent long-term dependence on welfare.
Critics argue that welfare can discourage people from taking up low-paid work, which is why work incentives form part of many schemes.

notes.h: Practical setting: schooling then and now
points: Ask an older relative how many years they attended school, how many children were in their class and whether they stayed on after the minimum school-leaving age.
Record the same details for a present-day young person and compare the answers.
Note which support services, such as special needs assistants and school completion programmes, were not available to the older relative.

keyTerms.definition: Income support paid by the state to people who are unemployed, sick, disabled, retired or caring for others.
An assessment of household income and savings that decides whether a payment is made and how much it is.
A payment made to everyone in a category, such as every child, without a means test.
Pay-related social insurance, paid by employees and employers, which funds contributory social welfare payments.
Education after second level, provided in universities, institutes of technology and colleges.
Education that gives adults who left school early a route to qualifications.
A school staff member who supports pupils with special educational needs in mainstream classes.
A card giving eligible people free GP visits and prescribed medicines.
An alternative admission pathway to third-level education for students from under-represented groups.

factCards.term: Three ways improved education supports family life
factCards.definition: Better parental help with learning, greater financial independence for women, and higher earning power that raises household living standards.

factCards.term: Four programmes or courses that help young people stay in education
factCards.definition: School Completion Programme, Leaving Certificate Applied, Youthreach and Transition Year.

factCards.term: Two types of social welfare payment
factCards.definition: Social insurance payments funded by PRSI contributions, and means-tested payments based on household income.

factCards.term: Three effects of welfare payments on family life
factCards.definition: They reduce child poverty, give older people financial independence, and help families cope with illness or unemployment.

questions.prompt: State two ways in which the state has improved the provision of education for children and young people in Ireland.
questions.model: Free second-level education introduced from 1967. A free pre-school year before primary school under the Early Childhood Care and Education scheme. Special needs assistants in mainstream classes. School Completion Programme for students at risk of leaving early.

questions.prompt: Explain how improvements in education and in social welfare have helped Irish families. Discuss one limitation of welfare support in your answer.
questions.model: Education: free second-level schooling and the abolition of third-level fees widened access, so more children complete school and continue into further study. Higher educational attainment raises employment prospects and earnings, which improves family living standards. Adult and second-chance education lets parents return to work, adding a second income. Support programmes such as the School Completion Programme and special needs assistants keep vulnerable pupils in school. Welfare: means-tested and universal payments give regular income to families with children, lone parents and low-paid workers; child benefit is paid per child regardless of income; medical cards give free GP visits to eligible families; old age pensions give older people independence. Limitation: payments can fail to lift a family out of poverty if they are low, and conditions such as job-seeking requirements or income thresholds can discourage some people from taking low-paid work.
